response.global_summary:
Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy is being explored as a treatment for glioblastoma (GBM), with research focusing on overcoming challenges such as the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and monitoring treatment response [0][2][4][8][9][10][12][13][16][17][24][25][27]. While some studies indicate the feasibility and preliminary efficacy of CAR-T cell therapy in GBM, with at least transient responses and acceptable adverse effects [11][12][15][25], the median overall survival (OS) in treated patients has ranged from **5.5 to 11.1 months** across various studies [3].

One significant challenge for CAR-T cell therapy in GBM is the penetration of the blood-brain barrier [0][2][4][8][10][12][13][16][17][24]. Emerging strategies to enhance CAR-T cell delivery and BBB penetration include locoregional administration [2][9][24], viral vectors, and nanotechnology-enabled platforms [2]. Physical modalities like focused ultrasound and thermal modulation can transiently disrupt the BBB to improve CAR-T cell therapy [0][4][24]. Despite these challenges, some findings suggest that CAR-T cells can be effectively delivered peripherally, rather than solely requiring direct intracranial administration, and that multi-antigen, regionally delivered products can induce measurable intracranial responses [12]. Preclinical studies, such as one using an aggressive orthotopic xenograft model of glioblastoma, have shown that GD2-CAR-T cells effectively infiltrated the brain and controlled tumor growth after intravenous administration [7].

Several clinical trials are investigating the safety and efficacy of various CAR-T cell constructs for glioblastoma. A Phase 1 trial is assessing the safety and preliminary efficacy of metabolically armed EGFRvIII CAR-T cell therapy for recurrent glioblastoma [5]. Another Phase 1 trial is evaluating the safety and efficacy of EGFRvIII-CAR T cells for glioblastoma patients with leptomeningeal disease [19]. The safety and feasibility of CART-EGFR-IL13Ra2 cells in patients with EGFR-amplified recurrent glioblastoma are also being evaluated in a Phase 1 clinical trial [20]. Additionally, a Phase 1 trial is assessing the safety and optimal dose of intracranial TGFβR2KO/IL13Rα2 CAR T-cells for recurrent/progressive glioblastoma or IDH-mutant astrocytoma [23]. A pilot Phase 1 study is determining the safety and efficacy of autologous anti-EGFRvIII CAR T cells in patients with recurrent glioblastoma multiforme [28]. GD2-specific 4SCAR-T cells have been found to be safe and well tolerated in glioblastoma patients, both with single and combined infusions, with **no severe adverse events** [11].

Monitoring treatment response in glioblastoma patients is another area of active research. Tumor in situ fluid circulating tumor DNA (TISF-ctDNA) can be used to monitor recurrent glioblastoma (rGBM) patients' response to combination therapy and guide treatment [1]. TISF-ctDNA positivity was identified in **62.2%** of glioblastoma patients in the early postsurgical period, indicating a high prevalence of molecular residual disease [22]. However, plasma cell-free tumor DNA (cf-tDNA) typically represents **less than 1%** of total cf-DNA due to the BBB, which limits its usefulness in practice and necessitates the development of highly sensitive detection methods [6]. Real-time imaging can be integrated with physical modalities for BBB disruption to enable dynamic monitoring of therapeutic responses [0].

Combination strategies are also being explored to enhance CAR-T cell efficacy. For instance, in immunodeficient and immunocompetent orthotopic GBM mice models, B7H3-targeted CAR-T cells alone failed to inhibit GBM growth, but achieved a durable antitumor response when combined with intratumoral administration of CXCL11-armed oncolytic adenoviruses [21].

key_findings.text: Physical modalities like focused ultrasound and thermal modulation can temporarily disrupt the blood-brain barrier to improve CAR-T cell therapy in glioblastoma, and real-time imaging can monitor responses [0][4][24].

Locoregional administration, viral vectors, and nanotechnology-enabled platforms are emerging delivery methods designed to enhance blood-brain barrier penetration and intratumoral retention of CAR-T cells for glioblastoma treatment [2][9][24].
CAR-T cell therapy for glioblastoma is considered feasible, showing at least transient responses and acceptable adverse effects [11][12][15][25].
Tumor in situ fluid circulating tumor DNA (TISF-ctDNA) can be used to monitor the response of recurrent glioblastoma patients to combination therapy and guide treatment [1].
Plasma cell-free tumor DNA (cf-tDNA) is generally limited in its usefulness for monitoring brain tumors due to the blood-brain barrier, as it typically represents less than 1% of total cf-DNA [6].
GD2-specific 4SCAR-T cells have demonstrated safety and good tolerability in glioblastoma patients, with no severe adverse events reported in a randomized controlled trial [11].
In preclinical glioblastoma xenograft models, GD2-CAR-T cells administered intravenously effectively infiltrated the brain and controlled tumor growth [7].

In mouse models of glioblastoma, B7H3-targeted CAR-T cells alone were insufficient to inhibit tumor growth but achieved a durable antitumor response when combined with intratumoral administration of CXCL11-armed oncolytic adenoviruses [21].
TISF-ctDNA positivity was observed in 62.2% of glioblastoma patients in the early postsurgical period, indicating a high prevalence of molecular residual disease [22].

evidence_gaps: The long-term efficacy and overall survival benefits of CAR-T cell therapy in glioblastoma patients are not definitively established across all studies, with reported median OS ranging from 5.5 to 11.1 months [3].
The optimal CAR-T cell constructs, target antigens, and delivery methods for consistent and durable responses in glioblastoma patients are still under investigation [2][5][19][20][23][28].

The specific impact of various BBB disruption techniques (e.g., focused ultrasound, thermal modulation) on CAR-T cell distribution, efficacy, and safety in human glioblastoma patients needs further clinical validation [0][4][24].

The clinical utility and optimal methods for monitoring CAR-T cell activity and tumor response using ctDNA in glioblastoma, particularly given the limitations of plasma cf-tDNA, require more research [1][6][22].
